subject: chemistry

items.q: A life cycle assessment of a product assesses its environmental impact in which stages?
items.correct: Extracting and processing raw materials, manufacturing and packaging, use, disposal
items.misconception: Manufacturing and packaging only, because that is the stage that uses the most energy
items.why: Manufacture is the stage students picture most easily, and it is the stage most often shown in textbook images and adverts. The word 'production' is also used loosely in everyday speech to mean the whole life of a product. Manufacturing and packaging is only one of the four stages. A product with a clean factory can still have a large overall impact from raw material extraction, from its use, or from its disposal.
items.random_wrong: Extraction, manufacture, use and disposal, with transport assessed as a separate stage

items.q: Why does a manufacturer carry out a life cycle assessment on a new product?
items.correct: To assess the environmental impact of the product at every stage of its life
items.misconception: To measure the pollution released by the factory where it is made
items.why: Manufacture is the stage students picture most easily, and it is the stage most often shown in textbook images and adverts. The word 'production' is also used loosely in everyday speech to mean the whole life of a product. Manufacturing and packaging is only one of the four stages. A product with a clean factory can still have a large overall impact from raw material extraction, from its use, or from its disposal.
items.random_wrong: To work out the profit that will be made from selling the product

items.q: A poly(ethene) carrier bag is made from crude oil. Which of these belongs to the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage of its LCA?
items.correct: Drilling for crude oil and cracking a fraction of it to obtain ethene
items.misconception: Wrapping the finished bags into bundles to be sent out to the shops
items.why: Students think of the LCA as being about the product, and packaging feels like a temporary extra rather than something that itself had to be made from raw materials. Packaging is made from raw materials, uses energy to manufacture and creates waste at disposal. The specification names it in the same stage as manufacturing, so it must be included.
items.random_wrong: Only the drilling of the crude oil, because processing is a later stage

items.q: Finished paper bags are put into cardboard boxes at the factory before being sent to shops. In an LCA of the paper bags, this belongs to:
items.correct: manufacturing and packaging, with the transport counted at that same stage
items.misconception: no stage at all, because packaging is thrown away and is not the product
items.why: Students think of the LCA as being about the product, and packaging feels like a temporary extra rather than something that itself had to be made from raw materials. Packaging is made from raw materials, uses energy to manufacture and creates waste at disposal. The specification names it in the same stage as manufacturing, so it must be included.
items.random_wrong: a separate transport stage, which is added on after the disposal stage

items.q: A glass milk bottle is washed and refilled every week. Which of these belongs to the 'use and operation during its lifetime' stage of its LCA?
items.correct: The water and the energy used to wash the bottle before refilling
items.misconception: Nothing, because a bottle is not powered and so has no use stage
items.why: Energy labels on appliances make the use stage very visible for electrical goods, so students assume the stage means 'energy used while switched on'. 'Use and operation during its lifetime' covers whatever the product consumes or causes while it is being used, including water and detergent for washing a reusable item, and how long it lasts before replacement.
items.random_wrong: The energy used to melt the sand and shape the bottle at the works

items.q: An empty steel food can is put out for kerbside recycling collection. In an LCA of the can, the impact of this is:
items.correct: part of the disposal stage, including transporting the collected cans
items.misconception: zero, because a can that is sent off for recycling is never disposed of
items.why: Recycling is presented as the environmentally good choice, so students treat it as having zero impact rather than as having a smaller impact than landfill. Recycling is a route for the product at the end of its useful life, not an escape from that stage. Lorries, sorting plants and remelting all use energy, so the impact is reduced rather than removed.
items.random_wrong: counted only within a separate stage covering all transport of the can

items.q: How are transport and distribution treated in a life cycle assessment?
items.correct: They are included at each stage of the life cycle
items.misconception: They form a fifth stage, placed after final disposal
items.why: Transport is listed at the end of the specification's list of stages, so it reads like another item on the list rather than a note about all of them. The wording is 'including transport and distribution at each stage'. Moving ore to a smelter, parts to a factory, goods to shops and waste to a tip are each counted within their own stage.
items.random_wrong: They are counted only when raw materials are moved

items.q: Which of these can be quantified fairly easily in a life cycle assessment?
items.correct: The volume of water used and the waste produced in manufacture
items.misconception: The harm done to a river by a pollutant released from the works
items.why: Data tables in exam questions give figures for pollutant emissions, so students assume the harm caused is equally measurable. Emissions can be measured; the damage they do must be valued. The mass of a pollutant released can be measured, but deciding how much weight to give that harm compared with, say, water use is a value judgement, which is why LCA is not purely objective.
items.random_wrong: The value that society places on protecting a nearby woodland

items.q: Why is a life cycle assessment not a purely objective process?
items.correct: Allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires judgements
items.misconception: Water use, energy use and waste produced cannot be measured at all
items.why: Data tables in exam questions give figures for pollutant emissions, so students assume the harm caused is equally measurable. Emissions can be measured; the damage they do must be valued. The mass of a pollutant released can be measured, but deciding how much weight to give that harm compared with, say, water use is a value judgement, which is why LCA is not purely objective.
items.random_wrong: Different scientists choose different stages of a product's life

items.q: A drinks company publishes an LCA of its bottle that covers the manufacturing stage only. Why is this a problem?
items.correct: A selective LCA can be used to reach a conclusion decided in advance
items.misconception: An abbreviated LCA uses the same data, so it gives the same result
items.why: Students think of a summary as a shorter account of the same thing, rather than as a selection that can change what the account shows. Leaving out a stage removes its impacts from the total. An assessment covering only manufacturing can make a product look far better than a full assessment would.
items.random_wrong: An LCA is scientific, so a conclusion drawn from it must be correct

items.q: An advert states that a paper cup is 'proven by science to be the greenest choice'. What is the best response to this claim?
items.correct: The LCA behind the claim may be selective and should be checked
items.misconception: The claim must be true, because an LCA is a scientific process
items.why: Attaching the word 'scientific' or 'proven' to a claim gives it authority, and students are not used to asking which stages a published figure covered. Ask what the LCA included: which stages, which impacts, and who paid for it. A company has an interest in the conclusion, and a selective LCA can be built to support it.
items.random_wrong: Paper products are always better, so the claim needs no checking

items.q: In a simple comparative LCA of plastic and paper shopping bags, which comparison is the fairest?
items.correct: The impact per use, taking account of how often each bag is used
items.misconception: The impact of making one bag, since reuse is not a part of an LCA
items.why: Students focus on the manufacturing figures given in the data table and treat 'one bag' as the fair unit of comparison, without noticing that the two bags do different amounts of work. Use and operation during its lifetime is one of the four stages. A bag used 20 times spreads its manufacturing impact over 20 uses, so impact per use, not per bag, is the fair comparison.
items.random_wrong: The cost of each bag to the shop, since price reflects resource use

items.q: Making a paper bag needs 4 times as much energy as making a plastic bag. On average a plastic bag is used 20 times and a paper bag 3 times. Which conclusion follows from these figures?
items.correct: Per use, the paper bag needs more energy than the plastic bag does
items.misconception: The paper bag is better, because paper is the more natural material
items.why: Campaigns against plastic waste make plastic the obvious villain, and the visible litter problem is easier to picture than the energy and water used to make paper. Making a paper bag typically uses more energy and water per bag, while a plastic bag is lighter and can often be used many more times. The comparison must cover all four stages before a conclusion is drawn.
items.random_wrong: The two bags are equal, since the number of uses is not counted

items.q: Reduction in use, reuse and recycling of materials by end users reduces:
items.correct: use of limited resources, use of energy sources, waste and impacts
items.misconception: waste only, because recycling a material uses no energy of its own
items.why: Recycling is taught as the solution to resource use, so students slide from 'uses less' to 'uses none'. The energy costs of collection and remelting are invisible to the end user. Compare, do not zero. Recycling aluminium uses far less energy than extracting it by electrolysis, but lorries, sorting plants and furnaces still consume energy from limited resources.
items.random_wrong: the price of the products, but not the quantity of raw material used

items.q: A family have the same glass bottle washed and refilled with milk each week. This is an example of:
items.correct: reuse, because the bottle itself is used again as a bottle
items.misconception: recycling, because the bottle is kept out of landfill waste
items.why: Both words contain the idea of 'using again', and students apply reuse to the material rather than to the object. Reuse keeps the object intact and uses it again for a purpose; recycling destroys the object and processes the material into something new. The specification gives both routes for glass bottles.
items.random_wrong: reduction in use, because fewer bottles are melted down

items.q: Which statement about the materials used to make everyday products is correct?
items.correct: Metals, glass, ceramics and most plastics come from limited materials
items.misconception: Only plastics are limited, because metal ores can always be mined
items.why: 'Running out' is taught most often about crude oil, and rock appears endlessly abundant. Students confuse how much of an element exists with how much is available in ore rich enough to be worth extracting. The specification lists metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics together as coming from limited raw materials. Useful ore and suitable sand are finite, and the easiest deposits are used first.
items.random_wrong: All of the energy for making these materials comes from unlimited sources

items.q: Which of these is an environmental impact of obtaining raw materials by quarrying and mining?
items.correct: Habitats are destroyed and waste rock and dust are produced on site
items.misconception: The only effect is that the landscape is left looking less attractive
items.why: The visual scar of a quarry is the impact students can see in a photograph, so it stands in for all the others. Appearance is one impact among several. Habitats are destroyed, waste rock and dust are produced, and the processes consume energy from limited resources.
items.random_wrong: There is no lasting impact, since the Earth's supply is unlimited

items.q: Used glass bottles are collected, crushed and melted to make glass jars. This is best described as:
items.correct: recycling, because the glass is processed into a new product
items.misconception: reuse, because the same glass is being used a second time
items.why: Both words contain the idea of 'using again', and students apply reuse to the material rather than to the object. Reuse keeps the object intact and uses it again for a purpose; recycling destroys the object and processes the material into something new. The specification gives both routes for glass bottles.
items.random_wrong: reduction in use, because fewer new jars need to be bought

items.q: What is the difference between reusing a glass bottle and recycling it?
items.correct: Reusing keeps the bottle whole; recycling melts it into new glass
items.misconception: There is no difference; crushing and melting glass counts as reuse
items.why: Both words contain the idea of 'using again', and students apply reuse to the material rather than to the object. Reuse keeps the object intact and uses it again for a purpose; recycling destroys the object and processes the material into something new. The specification gives both routes for glass bottles.
items.random_wrong: Recycling means the melted glass has to be made into bottles again

items.q: How are metals recycled?
items.correct: They are melted and then recast or reformed into new products
items.misconception: They must first be separated into completely pure single metals
items.why: Students transfer the rule that impurities weaken or contaminate a substance, learned in purity and separation work, to every recycling situation. Where the final product needs a precise composition, careful separation is required; where it does not, mixed scrap can be melted together. Scrap steel added to a blast furnace does not need the same sorting as scrap for a high-specification alloy.
items.random_wrong: They are heated with carbon to reduce them back into the metal

items.q: How much separation of scrap metal is needed before it is recycled?
items.correct: It depends on the material and the properties the product needs
items.misconception: Complete separation is always required before any metal is melted
items.why: Students transfer the rule that impurities weaken or contaminate a substance, learned in purity and separation work, to every recycling situation. Where the final product needs a precise composition, careful separation is required; where it does not, mixed scrap can be melted together. Scrap steel added to a blast furnace does not need the same sorting as scrap for a high-specification alloy.
items.random_wrong: None is ever needed, because melting removes all the other metals

items.q: Why is some scrap steel added to iron from a blast furnace?
items.correct: It cuts the amount of iron that must be extracted from iron ore
items.misconception: It removes the need for any iron ore to be used in the process
items.why: Students read 'reduce the amount' as 'remove the need for'. The wording that scrap is added to iron from a blast furnace is also skimmed, so the ore route is forgotten. The scrap is added to iron that has already come from the blast furnace, so ore is still being used. The benefit is that less iron has to be extracted from ore than would otherwise be needed.
items.random_wrong: It lets the scrap be used without separating any of it beforehand

items.q: A town council wants to reduce the use of limited resources. Which action would achieve this?
items.correct: Setting up a scheme to collect and refill glass milk bottles
items.misconception: Switching to newly made plastic bottles, as plastic is unlimited
items.why: 'Running out' is taught most often about crude oil, and rock appears endlessly abundant. Students confuse how much of an element exists with how much is available in ore rich enough to be worth extracting. The specification lists metals, glass, building materials, clay ceramics and most plastics together as coming from limited raw materials. Useful ore and suitable sand are finite, and the easiest deposits are used first.
items.random_wrong: Sending household waste to landfill rather than to an incinerator

items.q: A council compares two ways of supplying drinks: refillable glass bottles that are collected and washed, or cans made from recycled aluminium. Which point belongs in a fair evaluation?
items.correct: Washing the bottles uses water and energy, which must be weighed
items.misconception: Recycling the cans uses no energy, so this option has no impact
items.why: Recycling is taught as the solution to resource use, so students slide from 'uses less' to 'uses none'. The energy costs of collection and remelting are invisible to the end user. Compare, do not zero. Recycling aluminium uses far less energy than extracting it by electrolysis, but lorries, sorting plants and furnaces still consume energy from limited resources.
items.random_wrong: Refilling a bottle counts as recycling, so the options are equal

items.q: What does the 'extracting and processing raw materials' stage include?
items.correct: It includes both obtaining the raw material and every process needed to turn it into a usable material, such as reducing an ore to a metal or converting crude oil into a polymer.
items.misconception: Extracting raw materials just means digging them out of the ground; turning them into a material is part of manufacturing.
items.why: The word 'extracting' is the one students notice, and 'processing' in the same phrase is skimmed over. Extraction of metals is also taught as its own topic, which makes it feel separate. The stage is named 'extracting and processing raw materials'. Both halves belong to stage 1, so smelting an ore or cracking a fraction of crude oil is counted here, not under manufacturing.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does an LCA give one definite answer about which product is better?
items.correct: No. Because allocating numerical values to pollutant effects requires value judgements, LCA is not a purely objective process and different assessors can reach different conclusions from the same product.
items.misconception: An LCA is a scientific calculation, so it produces one correct score and any two assessments should agree.
items.why: Students associate anything with numbers in it with objectivity, and the phrase 'assessment' sounds like a measurement rather than a judgement. Parts of an LCA are measured, but the weighting given to different pollutant effects is a judgement. Disagreement between two LCAs does not automatically mean one contains an arithmetic mistake.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Are reduction in use, reuse and recycling the same thing?
items.correct: They are three different actions. Reduction in use means using fewer products; reuse means using the same product again as it is; recycling means processing the material into something new. All three reduce the use of limited resources, energy, waste and environmental impacts.
items.misconception: They all mean 'being green', so any of the three words can be used for any action that keeps something out of landfill.
items.why: The three words appear together as a slogan, which blurs the differences between them, and 'recycling' is used loosely in everyday speech for putting anything in a green bin. Check what happens to the object. Refilling a bottle is reuse; crushing and melting it is recycling; buying one large bottle instead of six small ones is reduction in use.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Must a recycled material be made back into the same product?
items.correct: No. Products that cannot be reused are recycled for a different use, and glass bottles can be crushed and melted to make different glass products.
items.misconception: Recycling means turning something back into what it was, so recycled bottles must become bottles again.
items.why: The recycling symbol suggests a closed loop, and the simplest classroom examples show a material returning to its original form. Recycled material is made into whatever product its properties and purity allow. This is why the amount of separation needed depends on the properties required of the final product.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Is only the raw material limited when a material such as glass or metal is produced?
items.correct: No. The raw materials are limited and, in addition, much of the energy for the processes comes from limited resources.
items.misconception: The ore or sand is the limited part; the energy for heating and melting is just electricity, which we can always make more of.
items.why: Electricity arrives at a socket with no visible fuel, so students separate it from the fossil fuels that generate much of it. The specification states that much of the energy for these processes comes from limited resources. Reducing the energy used, for example by recycling rather than extracting, conserves those resources too.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.10.2 Life cycle assessment and recycling
